13:4.headline: They 'cried out', meaning they were called together
13:4.body: צעק usually means to cry out. Metzudat Zion says here it means to gather at a crier's shout, and the Aramaic translates 'they assembled'.

sources.quote: ויצעקו. ענין אסיפה הבאה בצעקת המאסף
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a gathering that comes from the shout of the one calling people together.

sources.quote: וְאִתְכְּנִישׁוּ עַמָא בָּתַר שָׁאוּל לְגִלְגָלָא
sources.says: Targum Jonathan translates: the people gathered after Saul to Gilgal.

13:6.headline: Hiding in thorn bushes, or in strongholds?
13:6.body: חוחים are thorns, and Metzudat Zion reads it that way: people hid among the thorn bushes. Radak follows the Aramaic and reads it as strongholds.

sources.quote: ובחוחים. בין הקוצים, כמו (שיר השירים ב ב): כשושנה בין החוחים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means among thorns, as in 'like a rose among the thorns'.

sources.quote: ובחוחים.  במצדות כמו שת"י ובמצדתא
sources.says: Radak says it means in strongholds, as Jonathan translates.

13:7.headline: Trembling, or hurrying after Saul?
13:7.body: חרד usually means to tremble with fear. Rashi reads it as 'hurried', and Metzudat Zion as hurrying in alarm, so the people rushed after Saul.

sources.quote: מִהֲרוּ לָלֶכֶת אַחֲרָיו
sources.says: Rashi says they hurried to follow him.

sources.quote: חרדו. מהרו בחרדה, כמו (לקמן טז ד): ויחרדו זקני העיר לקראתו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says they hurried in alarm, as when the town elders hurried to meet Samuel.

13:12.headline: 'I held myself back', or 'I forced myself'?
13:12.body: התאפק usually means to hold yourself back. Rashi and Radak say Saul forced himself to act against his wish to wait; Malbim says Saul meant he held back from starting the battle and only brought the offering.

sources.quote: נִתְחַזַּקְתִּי עַל רְצוֹנִי, שֶׁהָיָה לִבִּי אוֹמֵר לְהַמְתִּין לְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says Saul means: I overpowered my own wish, since my heart told me to wait for you.

sources.quote: כי כל לשון התאפקות לחזק לבו לעבור על רצונו
sources.says: Radak says the word always means steeling one's heart to go against one's own wish.

sources.quote: לשון ואתאפק בא תמיד על שמונע את עצמו מעשות איזה דבר לא על העושה
sources.says: Malbim asks why the word is used, since it always means holding back from doing something, not doing it.

sources.quote: שבכ"ז התאפקתי ולא התחלתי במלחמה
sources.says: Malbim answers that Saul meant he held back and did not start the battle.

13:20.headline: The same word twice: a plow, then a craftsman's tool
13:20.body: The verse lists מחרשתו twice. Metzudat Zion and Radak say the first is a plow, and the second a craftsman's tool, from חרש, 'craftsman', as in 'a carpenter'.

sources.quote: מחרשתו. כלי המחרישה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the first מחרשתו is a plowing tool.

sources.quote: מחרשתו. כלי אומנות, כמו (ישעיהו מד יג): חרש עצים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the second מחרשתו is a craftsman's tool, as in 'a woodworker'.

sources.quote: מחרשתו. כלי אומנות מן חרש עצים חרש אבן
sources.says: Radak says the second is a craftsman's tool, from 'worker in wood, worker in stone', though the Aramaic seems to take it as a plow too.

13:21.headline: A file with 'many mouths' for sharpening tools
13:21.body: Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion read הפצירה פים as 'many mouths': a file with many sharp edges. They tie הפצירה to ויפצר, 'he pressed hard', which they read as 'many'.

sources.quote: שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהּ הַפְצַר פִּיּוֹת, כְּלוֹמַר פִּיּוֹת וְחִדּוּדִים הַרְבֵּה
sources.says: Rashi says it is a file with many mouths, that is, many sharp edges, used to sharpen plows.

sources.quote: הפצירה. ענין רבוי, כמו (בראשית יט ג): ויפצר בם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means 'many', as in 'he pressed them hard'.

sources.quote: ופי' פצירה רבה מלשון ויפצר בו שהוא רבוי דברים ותחנונים
sources.says: Radak says פצירה means 'much', from ויפצר, which means many words and pleas.

13:22.headline: Only Saul and Jonathan had swords, and even those by a miracle
13:22.body: Only Saul and Jonathan had a sword. Rashi says even theirs came by a miracle, and Radak cites a teaching that an angel provided them.

sources.quote: וַתִּמָּצֵא לְשָׁאוּל. עַל יְדֵי נֵס
sources.says: Rashi says the weapon was found for Saul by a miracle.

sources.quote: אף בידם לא היה אלא שהמלאך המציאה להם
sources.says: Radak cites a teaching that even they had none, and an angel provided them.

13:23.headline: Raiders, guards, or officers?
13:23.body: Rashi gives two readings: raiders who run out after plunder, or guards posted to keep anyone from leaving. Radak and Metzudat Zion follow the Aramaic and read it as army officers.

sources.quote: הֵם הַפּוֹשְׁטִים וְרָצִים אַחַר הַשָּׁלָל אֶל הָעִיר
sources.says: Rashi says they are troops who spread out and run after plunder.

sources.quote: הֵם נְצִיבִים לִשְׁמֹר שֶׁלֹּא יֵצְאוּ מִן הָעִיר
sources.says: Rashi also says they are posted guards who keep people from leaving the town.

sources.quote: פי' שרי החיל וכן תירגם יונתן אסטרטיג
sources.says: Radak says it means army officers, as Jonathan translates.

sources.quote: מצב. תרגם יונתן: אסטרטיג
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says Jonathan translates it as an officer, the same word he uses for the נציב in verses 3 and 4.

14:1.headline: 'This one', or 'that one over there'?
14:1.body: Metzudat Zion reads הלז as simply 'this'. Rashi says that everywhere in the Bible הלז means the thing across from you, the one you point at with a finger.

sources.quote: כָּל ״הַלָּז״ וְ״לָזֶה״ שֶׁבַּמִּקְרָא אֵינוֹ לְשׁוֹן ״הַזֶּה״, אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן דָּבָר שֶׁכְּנֶגְדוֹ, וְהוּא מַרְאֵהוּ בְּאֶצְבַּע
sources.says: Rashi says הלז in Scripture never means 'this', but the thing opposite, which one points to with a finger.

sources.quote: הלז. הזה, כמו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says הלז means 'this'.

14:4.headline: The slippery rock Jonathan climbed on hands and feet
14:4.body: Radak says we do not know what the rock names mean, but the Aramaic Targum calls בוצץ 'the slippery one'. Radak thinks this is the rock Jonathan climbed, which is why he needed his hands as well as his feet.

sources.quote: לא נודע אצלינו ענין השמות אלא שי"ת בוצץ משרועיתא מקום חלקלק
sources.says: Radak says the meaning of the names is not known to us, but the Targum renders בוצץ as a slippery place.

sources.quote: דרך הסלע ששמו בוצץ שת"י משרועית' והיה חלקלק לפיכך היה צריך לסמוך על ידיו ועל רגליו
sources.says: Radak says Jonathan went up by the rock called בוצץ, which was slippery, so he had to use his hands and feet.

sources.quote: וְשׁוּם חֲדָא מַשְׁרוּעִיתָא
sources.says: The Targum names one rock 'the slippery one'.

14:5.headline: A rock that stood up, sloped, or dropped sheer
14:5.body: Metzudat Zion reads מצוק as 'standing', from the verb for setting something down. Rashi says the rock sloped up toward Michmash, while Malbim says its face was smooth, so no one could climb it.

sources.quote: מצוק. מוצב, וכן (שמואל ב טו כד): ויציקו את ארון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means 'set up', as when they set down the ark in II Samuel 15:24.

sources.quote: מְשֻׁפָּע וְעוֹלֶה מִצַּד צָפוֹן אֶל מִכְמָשׂ
sources.says: Rashi says the rock sloped and rose from the north toward Michmash.

sources.quote: שהיה שם חלק ושוה, שאי אפשר לרדת ממנו
sources.says: Malbim says that side was smooth and even, so no one could climb down it.

14:6.headline: Nothing holds God back, whether the army is big or small
14:6.body: This word appears only here, and Metzudat Zion links it to Sarah's 'God has kept me from bearing'. Malbim explains that in nature a force must be bigger than what resists it, but nothing resists God, so many or few makes no difference.

sources.quote: מעצור. ענין מניעה, כמו (בראשית טז ב): עצרני ה׳ מלדת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means holding back, as in Genesis 16:2.

sources.quote: כי בכחות הטבעיים צריך שכח המתגבר יגדל מן הכח השני המנוצח
sources.says: Malbim says that among natural forces, the winning force must be greater than the one it beats.

sources.quote: לא כן אצל ה', שאין שום כח טבעי יעצור בעדו
sources.says: He says this is not so for God, since no natural force can hold him back.

14:15.headline: A 'trembling of God': a huge panic, or one God sent
14:15.body: Adding 'God' to a word can just mean 'very great', like 'cedars of God' in Psalms, says Metzudat David. Radak reads it plainly: the panic came from God, since only two men were fighting them.

sources.quote: כי כאשר ירצה להגדיל דבר מה, סומכו למלת ׳אל׳
sources.says: Metzudat David says that to make something sound great, the text attaches the word for God to it.

sources.quote: כלומר כי מהאלהים באה להם החרדה
sources.says: Radak says the fear came to them from God.

sources.quote: חרדה גדולה כטעם אש אלהים הררי אל או יהיה הרצון בו שהחרדה היתה מסובבת מהש"י
sources.says: Ralbag gives both readings: a great fear, or a fear caused by God.

14:16.headline: An army becomes a 'crowd' once it falls apart
14:16.body: Malbim says that while soldiers keep their ranks, the text calls them a camp or an army. Once panic breaks them up, they are called המון, a noisy crowd with no order.

sources.quote: כי המחנה כל זמן שעומדת על דגלה וסדרה
sources.says: Malbim says a camp is called a camp as long as it keeps its banner and order.

sources.quote: ששם המון מורה על קיבוץ בלתי מסודר כחוקי סדרי המלחמה
sources.says: He says המון means a gathering that is not in battle order.

14:16.headline: 'Coming this way', or 'being beaten down'?
14:16.body: Rashi reads והלם as הלום, 'here': the crowd moved toward Israel. Metzudat Zion and Radak take it from the verb for striking, as when Yael struck Sisera: the crowd kept being beaten.

sources.quote: נָמוֹג מִמְּקוֹמוֹ וַיֵּלֶךְ, וְקָרַב הֲלוֹם לְצַד יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says the crowd moved from its place and came closer, here, toward Israel.

sources.quote: ענין הכאה, כמו (שופטים ה כו): והלמה סיסרא
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means striking, as in 'she struck Sisera'.

sources.quote: מן והלמה סיסרא פי' הלוך והשבר
sources.says: Radak says it comes from 'she struck Sisera': they kept going and breaking.

14:18.headline: 'Bring the ark' means bring the means of asking God
14:18.body: Saul wanted to ask God what was happening. Rashi and Radak say 'the ark' here means the Urim and Tummim, which the priest used to ask God, not the ark itself.

sources.quote: הַגִּישָׁה אֲרוֹן הָאֱלֹהִים. אוּרִים וְתֻמִּים
sources.says: Rashi says 'bring the ark of God' means the Urim and Tummim.

sources.quote: ר"ל האפוד האורים והתומים שהיו עם ארון האלהים לשאול בהם על יהונתן
sources.says: Radak says it means the ephod with the Urim and Tummim, to ask about Jonathan.

15:3.headline: Why kill even the oxen and sheep?
15:3.body: Rashi says the Amalekites were sorcerers who could disguise themselves as animals. Radak says no animal could be left to be shown off as Amalek's spoil, since Amalek's memory had to be wiped out.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיוּ בַּעֲלֵי כְּשָׁפִים, וּמְשַׁנִּין עַצְמָן וְדוֹמִין לִבְהֵמָה
sources.says: Rashi says they were sorcerers who changed themselves to look like animals.

sources.quote: כי אם יחיו מהם שור או חמור יאמרו זה היה משלל עמלק
sources.says: Radak says a surviving ox or donkey would be pointed to as Amalek's spoil, keeping its memory alive.

sources.quote: שלא יאמר זה השור היה משלל עמלק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra gives the same reason: so no one says 'this ox was Amalek's'.

15:5.headline: Saul 'fought in the valley', or argued about it
15:5.body: Rashi reads וירב as 'fought in the valley', and Radak as 'set an ambush'. The rabbis heard ריב, 'argue': Saul argued that if one dead man needs a calf's neck broken in a valley, so many deaths must be far worse.

sources.quote: וַיִּלָּחֵם בַּנַּחַל וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ אָמְרוּ (יומא כב ב): עַל עִסְקֵי נַחַל רָב וְדָן אֶת עַצְמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it means he fought in the valley, and brings the rabbis: he argued with himself over the law of the valley.

sources.quote: וירב בנחל. שרשו ארב משפטו ויארב
sources.says: Radak says the root may be ארב, to lie in ambush, or ריב, to fight.

15:9.headline: Saul 'spared' them because he thought he knew better
15:9.body: Malbim separates three words for pity. He says חמל is a judgment of the mind, not a feeling: Saul decided that destroying everything was not right.

sources.quote: אבל החמלה הוא ענין מחשביי, שחושב שאין מן הראוי והיושר להשחיתם
sources.says: Malbim says חמלה is a thought: judging that it is not right to destroy something.

sources.quote: לפי שסופם לחמול כמו שאמר ויחמול שאול
sources.says: Radak says God warned 'do not spare' because they would end up sparing, as this verse says.

15:9.headline: A word with no parallel: the 'doubled', fattest animals
15:9.body: Rashi says the word appears nowhere else. He reads it from משנה, 'double': animals doubled in flesh and fat, and Radak adds yearlings or second-born.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן ׳מִשְׁנִים׳, כְּמוֹ (בראשית מג:יב): ״כֶּסֶף מִשְׁנֶה״, עַל שֵׁם שֶׁהוּא כָּפוּל בְּבָשָׂר וּבְשׁוּמָן
sources.says: Rashi says it is from 'double', since the animal is doubled in flesh and fat.

sources.quote: ויש לפרש המשנים הכבשים בני שנה והכרים גדולים משנה, ויש מפרשים המשנים שהם שניים לבטן
sources.says: Radak also offers year-old lambs, or animals born second.

15:9.headline: Livestock called 'work'
15:9.body: מלאכה usually means work. Radak and Metzudat Zion say it means livestock here, because herds are what a herdsman works at.

sources.quote: המקנה, נקראת מלאכה, לפי שבו עבודת האדם בעל המקנה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says livestock is called מלאכה because its owner works with it.

sources.quote: כי כל דבר שיתעסק בו האדם נקרא מלאכה
sources.says: Radak says anything a person busies himself with is called מלאכה.

15:11.headline: Can God regret? 'I regret' set against 'He does not regret'
15:11.body: God says נחמתי, 'I regret', yet verse 29 says He does not regret. Ibn Ezra says the Torah speaks in human terms, and Rashi reads it as 'I have had a new thought about Saul's kingship'.

sources.quote: חלילה להנחם השם רק דברה תורה כלשון בני אדם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God does not truly regret; the Torah speaks in human language, and he points to this verse and verse 29.

sources.quote: מַחֲשָׁבָה עָלְתָה בְּלִבִּי עַל מַלְכוּת שָׁאוּל
sources.says: Rashi says it means a thought rose in God's heart about Saul's kingship.

sources.quote: תָּבֵית בְּמֵימְרִי
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'I have turned back in My word'.

15:15.headline: Saul says 'your God', not 'our God'
15:15.body: Saul tells Samuel the animals are for 'the LORD your God'. Radak says he said 'your' to honor Samuel, as one speaks of a great man's God as his own.

sources.quote: ואמר אלהיך לכבוד שמואל להגדיל מעלתו
sources.says: Radak says Saul said 'your God' to honor Samuel and raise his standing.

15:17.headline: 'Head of the tribes': the Targum recalls Benjamin at the sea
15:17.body: Samuel calls Saul ראש, 'head', of Israel's tribes. The Targum, quoted by Rashi, says Saul's tribe of Benjamin crossed into the sea first, and that merit made him king.

sources.quote: שִׁבְטָא דְבִנְיָמִין עֲבַר בְּיַמָּא בְּרֵישׁ כָּל עַמָּא
sources.says: Rashi quotes the Targum: the tribe of Benjamin crossed the sea at the head of the people.

sources.quote: בְּרַם זְכוּת שִׁבְטָא דְבִנְיָמִין אֲבוּךְ גָרְמָא לָךְ
sources.says: The Targum says the merit of Saul's tribe, Benjamin, brought him the kingship.

15:19.headline: Saul 'swooped' on the spoil like a bird of prey
15:19.body: ותעט is rare. Rashi ties it to עיט, the bird of prey in Genesis 15:11, and Metzudat Zion says it means flying fast, while Radak reads 'you turned aside'.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ וַתָּעָף, לְשׁוֹן עַיִט
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'you flew', from עיט, a bird of prey.

sources.quote: ענין פריחה, כמו (לקמן כה יד): ויעט בהם, ורוצה לומר מהירות ההליכה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means flying, that is, rushing.

sources.quote: שהיא כמו ותסר או ותטה
sources.says: Radak says it means 'you turned aside'.

15:21.headline: 'The first of the banned things': the best, or before the ban?
15:21.body: Rashi and Radak read ראשית as 'the best', as in 'the first of the oils'. Targum Jonathan reads it as time: the people took the animals before they were banned.

sources.quote: רֵאשִׁית הַחֵרֶם. מֵיטַב הַחֵרֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it means the best of the banned things.

sources.quote: וי"ת לשון תחלה קדם דיחרמון כלומר טרם שיחרימו
sources.says: Radak brings the Targum, which reads it as 'before they banned them'.

sources.quote: קֳדָם דְיַחְרְמוּן
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'before they would ban them'.

15:22.headline: God wants listening itself; offerings are only a means
15:22.body: Malbim says חפץ is real desire, unlike mere approval: God desires obedience for itself, and offerings only as a way to it. Maimonides quotes this verse to show offerings are not the goal and God does not need them.

sources.quote: כי יש הבדל בין חפץ ובין רצון, שהחפץ הוא תכונה נפשיית
sources.says: Malbim says חפץ, desire, differs from רצון, approval, and God desires obedience itself.

sources.quote: והובהר להם שאין הם המטרה המכוונת כשלעצמם ושה' אינו צריך להם
sources.says: Maimonides says the prophets made clear that offerings are not the goal in themselves and God does not need them.

15:23.headline: Pushing back with many words is like idol worship
15:23.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra read הפצר as piling on words, as in 'he pressed him' in Genesis 33:11. Malbim says Samuel means Saul's stubborn refusal to admit his sin.

sources.quote: הַפְצַר. לְשׁוֹן תּוֹסֶפֶת, וְכֵן (בראשית לג:יא): ״וַיִּפְצַר בּוֹ״, הִרְבָּה עָלָיו דְּבָרִים
sources.says: Rashi says it means adding, as when Jacob pressed many words on Esau.

sources.quote: וזאת המלה רבוי דברים כטעם פיוסים, וכן "ואון ותרפים" הפצר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word means many words of urging, and cites this verse.

sources.quote: שאם מפציר ומתחזק בדעתו ואינו מודה על פשעו
sources.says: Malbim says it is one who insists on his view and does not admit his sin.

15:24.headline: 'I feared the people': Rashi says it was Doeg
15:24.body: Saul blames 'the people'. Rashi says he meant Doeg the Edomite, who counted as much as all of them.

sources.quote: דּוֹאֵג הָאֲדוֹמִי, שֶׁהָיָה חָשׁוּב כֻּלָּם
sources.says: Rashi says 'the people' means Doeg the Edomite, who was worth all of them.

15:27.headline: Whose robe was torn? The sages disagree
15:27.body: The plain reading is that Saul grabbed Samuel's robe and it tore. A midrash in Rashi says Samuel tore Saul's robe as a sign: whoever cuts the corner of your robe will rule after you, as David later did.

sources.quote: יֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים: מְעִילוֹ שֶׁל שְׁמוּאֵל קָרַע שָׁאוּל. וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים: מְעִילוֹ שֶׁל שָׁאוּל קָרַע שְׁמוּאֵל
sources.says: Rashi brings a dispute: some say Saul tore Samuel's robe, others that Samuel tore Saul's.

sources.quote: שאול החזיק בכנף מעיל שמואל כדי שישוב עמו
sources.says: Radak says Saul held Samuel's robe so he would come back with him.

15:28.headline: A torn robe becomes a torn kingdom
15:28.body: The robe tears in verse 27, and Samuel says God has torn the kingdom from Saul. Metzudat David says the tear is a sign, and Malbim says an act joined to a prophecy shows the decree is already final.

sources.quote: הקריעה ההיא, היא לסימן שכבר קרע ה׳
sources.says: Metzudat David says the tearing is a sign that God has already torn the kingdom away.

sources.quote: קריעת המעיל שהיא פעולה שנעשית עם הנבואה מורה שאינה גזרה עתידית
sources.says: Malbim says the tearing, an act done with the prophecy, shows the decree is not for the future but already done.

15:29.headline: Netzach Yisrael: Israel's Eternal One, its Strength, or its Life-blood
15:29.body: נצח can mean forever, victory, strength or blood. Rashi reads 'Israel's victory', Metzudat Zion 'Israel's strength', and Ralbag 'Israel's life', since blood is called נצח.

sources.quote: שֶׁהוּא נִצְחוֹנוֹ שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says God is Israel's victory.

sources.quote: ועל המקום יאמר, שהוא חוזקן של ישראל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means strength: God is Israel's strength.

sources.quote: כמו הדם שהוא חיי הגוף כי הדם יקרא נצח
sources.says: Ralbag says God is Israel's life, as blood is the body's life, and blood is called נצח.

sources.quote: כי ה' הנצחי שמתנאי נצחיותו שלא ימצא בו שום שינוי
sources.says: Malbim reads it as the Eternal One, who by being eternal does not change.

15:29.headline: God does not change His mind the way people do
15:29.body: Here Samuel says God is not a man, to regret. Metzudat David squares this with verse 11: God Himself does not change, but the change comes from the person He deals with.

sources.quote: מפאת עצמו אין בו שינוי להנחם, אבל השינוי בא מפאת המקבל, ולזה נאמר בשאול נחמתי
sources.says: Metzudat David says God does not change in Himself; the change comes from the receiver, which is why verse 11 says 'I regret'.

sources.quote: אבל הקב"ה אין בו שנוי חפץ
sources.says: Radak says God does not change His will, unlike a person.

15:32.headline: Agag came 'delicately', or in chains
15:32.body: The Targum and Rashi read מעדנת as 'pampered', walking like a king. Metzudat Zion and Ralbag read 'in bonds', from the same word in Job 38:31, and Radak gives both.

sources.quote: יוֹנָתָן תִּרְגֵּם: ״אֲגַג מְפַנְּקָא״
sources.says: Rashi quotes the Targum: Agag the pampered.

sources.quote: מעדנות. ענין קשור, כמו (איוב לח לא): התקשר מעדנות כימה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means bound, as in Job 38:31.

sources.quote: כתרגומו מפנקא כלו' הלך אליו כמהלך המלכים בתענוג
sources.says: Radak follows the Targum, saying Agag walked like a king, at ease, and also brings the reading 'in chains'.

15:32.headline: Has death's bitterness passed, or arrived?
15:32.body: Ralbag reads סר as 'gone': Agag thought he would be spared. Rashi and Radak read it as 'come near': Agag knew he would die.

sources.quote: אמר באמת סר מרירות המות כי נפלתי ביד מי שראוי שירחם עלי
sources.says: Ralbag says Agag thought death's bitterness had passed because he had come before a merciful man.

sources.quote: בֶּאֱמֶת יָדַעְתִּי כִּי סָר וְקָרֵב עָלַי מְרִירַת הַמָּוֶת
sources.says: Rashi says Agag meant the bitterness of death had come near him.

sources.quote: הגיע מרירות המות ידע כי להמיתו הביאו אותו אליו
sources.says: Radak says death's bitterness had arrived; Agag knew he was brought to be killed.

16:1.headline: Saul was anointed from a flask, David from a horn
16:1.body: God tells Samuel to fill his horn with oil. Malbim says Saul was anointed from a flask and his reign did not last, and Radak says this horn was kept for anointing the kings of David's line.

sources.quote: כי שאול נמשח בפך ולכן לא נמשך מלכותו
sources.says: Malbim says Saul was anointed from a flask, so his kingdom did not continue.

sources.quote: לפי שהיה הקרן הזה מזומן למשוח בו מלכי בית דוד
sources.says: Radak says this horn was set aside for anointing the kings of David's house.

16:1.headline: 'A king for Me', not just a king for Israel
16:1.body: God says He has found among Jesse's sons a king לי, 'for Me'. Radak says this means a king who will serve God, unlike Saul, and Malbim adds that what is 'for Me' lasts forever.

sources.quote: ולא אמר לישראל מלך ר"ל לי שיהיה לעבודתי
sources.says: Radak says God did not say 'a king for Israel' but 'for Me', a king who will serve Him.

sources.quote: וכמ"ש בספרי כל מקום שנאמר לי קיים לעולם
sources.says: Malbim quotes the Sifre: wherever 'for Me' is said, it lasts forever.

16:2.headline: The calf as cover: the town feared an unsolved killing
16:2.body: God tells Samuel to bring a calf and say he came to offer it. Ralbag brings a reading that a calf would hint at the rite for an unsolved killing, and Malbim says that is why the elders trembled in verse 4.

sources.quote: להעיר על שכבר נמצא חלל באדמה לא נודע מי הכהו יהיה הולך לערוף העגלה
sources.says: Ralbag brings a teacher's view that the calf would suggest a body had been found and Samuel was going to perform the calf rite.

sources.quote: חרדו אולי נמצא חלל באדמה הקרובה אל בית לחם ובא לערוף העגלה בנחל
sources.says: Malbim says the elders trembled because they thought a body had been found near Bethlehem.

sources.quote: ולמדו רבותינו ז"ל מזה הפסוק שמצוה לשנות בדברי שלום
sources.says: Radak says the rabbis learned from this verse that one may change one's words for the sake of peace.

16:4.headline: The elders 'trembled', or hurried out to meet him
16:4.body: Rashi reads ויחרדו as 'hurried out', and Radak adds the Targum's 'gathered'. Radak also reads 'trembled': they feared someone in town had sinned badly enough to bring the prophet.

sources.quote: מִהֲרוּ לָצֵאת לִקְרָאתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says they hurried out to meet him.

sources.quote: ויש לפרשו לשון חרדה כי תמהו על בואו ופחדו אולי היה בעיר מי שחטא חטא גדול
sources.says: Radak says it can mean fear: they wondered why he came and feared someone in the city had sinned badly.

16:6.headline: 'Surely His anointed': Eliab, or Saul?
16:6.body: Radak says Samuel took tall, handsome Eliab, the firstborn, for the new king. Ralbag and Malbim bring a reading that Samuel meant Saul, the king already anointed, and hoped God would keep him.

sources.quote: כי חשב כי זה הוא המלך שצוהו האל למשוח לפי שהיה בכור בבני ישי
sources.says: Radak says Samuel thought Eliab was the one to anoint because he was Jesse's firstborn.

sources.quote: יש שפירשו שהוא כאשר ראה אליאב בלתי ראוי למלוכה אמר על שאול כי נגד ה' משיחו
sources.says: Ralbag brings a view that, seeing Eliab unfit, Samuel said this about Saul.

sources.quote: כי משיחו שהוא שאול שנמשח מכבר עודהו נגד ה'
sources.says: Malbim reads 'His anointed' as Saul, still standing before God.

16:7.headline: Samuel called himself 'the seer', and here he does not see
16:7.body: God says people see only what meets the eye. Rashi hears a rebuke: Samuel once told Saul 'I am the seer', and here God shows him he does not see.

sources.quote: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁקָּרָאתָ לְעַצְמְךָ רוֹאֶה, שֶׁאָמַרְתָּ לְשָׁאוּל (שמואל א ט:יט): ״אָנֹכִי הָרוֹאֶה״, כָּאן אֲנִי מוֹדִיעֲךָ שֶׁאֵינְךָ רוֹאֶה
sources.says: Rashi says that though Samuel called himself 'the seer', God tells him here that he does not see.

16:7.headline: Why Eliab was rejected: Rashi says his temper
16:7.body: God says He has rejected Eliab despite his looks. Rashi says it was because he was quick to anger, as when he flared at David in 17:28.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁכַּעְסָן הוּא, כְּמָה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שמואל א יז:כח): ״וַיִּחַר אַף אֱלִיאָב בְּדָוִד״
sources.says: Rashi says Eliab was rejected because he had a temper, as shown when he grew angry at David.

sources.quote: ידע לבב אליאב כי איננו ישר
sources.says: Radak says God knew Eliab's heart was not upright.

16:10.headline: Seven sons pass by, and David makes eight
16:10.body: Seven of Jesse's sons pass before Samuel while David is with the sheep, but Chronicles counts seven with David. Metzudat David brings a midrash about an eighth son, Elihu.

sources.quote: בדברי הימים (א ב טו) לא חשב כי אם שבעה עם דוד, שנאמר: דוד השביעי. ובמדרש יש שהיה לישי עוד בן, ושמו אליהו
sources.says: Metzudat David notes Chronicles counts seven sons including David, and a midrash adds a son named Elihu.

16:11.headline: 'The youngest stayed behind': a form found only here
16:11.body: The verb is usually נשאר. Radak says this is its only use in the simple form, and Malbim says it shows David stayed behind on his own.

sources.quote: פועל עומד כמו נשאר וזה לבדו מן הקל
sources.says: Radak says it means 'remained', and this is the only time it appears in this form.

sources.quote: וישי התנצל שדוד שאר מעצמו (ולכן בא פה פעל שאר בקל, ובנינו תמיד בנפעל)
sources.says: Malbim says Jesse explained that David stayed behind by himself, which is why this unusual form is used.

16:12.headline: Ruddy like Esau: Samuel feared a man of blood
16:12.body: אדמוני, 'ruddy', is also the word for Esau at birth. Malbim brings the rabbis: Samuel feared David would shed blood like Esau, and God answered that David would kill only by the court's ruling.

sources.quote: כיון שראה שמואל את דוד אדמוני נתירא אמר זה שופך דמים כעשו, א"ל הקב"ה עם יפה עינים, עשו עשה מדעת עצמו, זה מדעת סנהדרין הוא הורג
sources.says: Malbim quotes the rabbis: Samuel feared the ruddy David would shed blood like Esau, and God said David would kill only by the court's decision.

16:12.headline: 'Ruddy, with beautiful eyes': why 'with' and not 'and'?
16:12.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion say עם here simply means 'and'. Malbim says the midrash reads it as 'with': the fine eyes, a sign of good sense, balance the ruddy nature.

sources.quote: עם יפה עינים. כמו ויפה עינים
sources.says: Radak says it means 'and beautiful eyes'.

sources.quote: ולפי דרש חכמינו זכרונם לברכה נכון מה שבא מלת עם יפה עינים תחת וי"ו החבור
sources.says: Malbim says the rabbis' reading explains why the verse says 'with' instead of 'and'.

16:13.headline: God's spirit on David: courage, or prophecy?
16:13.body: Rashi calls it a spirit of might, the Targum a spirit of prophecy, and Radak says it was both. Maimonides calls it the first step toward prophecy, a drive to do great deeds, which is why David faced the lion, the bear and the Philistine.

sources.quote: וַתִּצְלַח רוּחַ ה׳. רוּחַ גְּבוּרָה
sources.says: Rashi says it was a spirit of might.

sources.quote: וּשְׁרַת רוּחַ נְבוּאָה מִן קֳדָם יְיָ עַל דָוִד
sources.says: The Targum says a spirit of prophecy from God rested on David.

sources.quote: כי בכלל רוח ה' רוח הקדש ורוח גבורה
sources.says: Radak says 'God's spirit' includes both holy spirit and a spirit of might.

sources.quote: וכן נלווה אל דוד כוח שכזה מאז נמשח בשמן המשחה
sources.says: Maimonides says this first degree of prophecy, a drive to great deeds, stayed with David from his anointing, so he faced the lion, bear and Philistine.

16:14.headline: Saul's 'evil spirit': a dark gloom that filled the empty place
16:14.body: Malbim says that when God's spirit left Saul, a dark spirit of gloom and fear took its place. In verse 15 he calls it an illness of melancholy, which music could ease.

sources.quote: ותחת רוח הנשגב ישכן בו רוח אחר שחוריי מלא בלהה ועצב, דאגה ובעתה
sources.says: Malbim says a dark spirit full of terror, sadness and worry took the place of the lofty spirit.

sources.quote: ונתהוה בו חולי המילאנקאלי
sources.says: Malbim says Saul developed the illness of melancholy.

sources.quote: רוח רעה. רוח מחריד ומרעיד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it was a spirit that made him shake with fear.

16:15.headline: An 'evil spirit of God': simply very strong, or sent by God
16:15.body: Metzudat David gives two readings. Adding אלהים can just mean 'great and strong', as in 'a trembling of God' (14:15), or it means the bad spirit came from God.

sources.quote: רצה לומר: רוח גדול וחזק, כי כשרוצה להגדיל דבר מה, סומכו למלת אלהים. וכן (לעיל יד טו) ותהי לחרדת אלהים או רצה לומר: רוח רעה הבאה מאלהים
sources.says: Metzudat David says 'of God' may only mean great and strong, or that the spirit came from God.

sources.quote: רוח אלהים אל שאול. פי' רוח רעה
sources.says: Radak says 'spirit of God' in verse 23 means the evil spirit.

16:20.headline: 'A donkey of bread': a donkey loaded with bread, or a heap
16:20.body: Radak and Ibn Ezra say a word is left out: a donkey loaded with bread. Radak also brings a reading of חמור as a heap of bread.

sources.quote: חמור טעון לחם ונאד מלא יין וכן תירגם יונתן טעון חמרא בלחם וי"מ חומר צבור
sources.says: Radak says it means a donkey loaded with bread, and some read it as a heap.

sources.quote: כי יתכן בכל לשון לקצר לאחוז דרך קצרה כמו חמור לחם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says every language can shorten a phrase, as 'a donkey of bread' does.

16:21.headline: David became Saul's armor-bearer, or got one of his own
16:21.body: The plain reading is that David became Saul's armor-bearer. Malbim also reads it the other way: David rose so high that he had his own armor-bearer, like a minister.

sources.quote: יש לפרש ג"כ שדוד נתעלה עד שהיה לו נושא כלים כדרך השרים
sources.says: Malbim says it can also mean David rose until he had an armor-bearer, as officers do.

sources.quote: נושא כלים. נושא כלי זיינו
sources.says: Radak reads it as David carrying Saul's weapons.

17:1.headline: Ephes-dammim: the place where bloodshed ended for Israel
17:1.body: אפס דמים is the name of the place where the Philistines camped. Radak cites a midrash on the name: one sage calls it a red field, and another says it is where the bloodshed (דמים) of Israel came to an end (אפס).

sources.quote: ובדרש רבי יוחנן אמר בחלק סמקתא ור' שמואל בר נחמן אמר שמשם פסקו דמים לישראל
sources.says: Radak cites the midrash: Rabbi Yochanan says it was a red field, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman says from there bloodshed stopped for Israel.

17:5.headline: A helmet, like the roast goat with its innards on its head
17:5.body: כובע is a helmet, also spelled קובע. Radak notes the Aramaic word for it, קולסא, and ties it to the sages' 'גדי מקולס', a Passover goat roasted with its innards hung over its head like a helmet.

sources.quote: ותרגומו קולסא ודומה לו בדברי רבותינו ז"ל גדי מקולס נקרא כן לפי כשהיו צולין הפסח היו תולין בני מעיו חוצה לו למעלה מראשו ונראה ככובע על הראש
sources.says: Radak says the Targum calls it קולסא, like the sages' 'helmeted goat', roasted with its innards above its head so it looked like a helmet.

sources.quote: כובע בכ״ף, וקובע בקו״ף, הוא אחד, והוא כלי מגן על הראש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says כובע with כ and קובע with ק are the same thing, a guard for the head.

17:6.headline: A 'forehead piece' on his legs?
17:6.body: מצחת comes from מצח, forehead, yet it sits on his legs. Radak says it is a metal plate over the legs, named after the plates girls wore on their foreheads. Rashi describes a bar from the helmet in front of the nose, long enough to reach his feet.

sources.quote: והוא שם מושאל מן מצח כי כן נושאות הנערות טס הזהב או כסף על מצחם
sources.says: Radak says the name is borrowed from מצח, forehead, since girls wore a gold or silver plate on the forehead.

sources.quote: כְּמִין יַד בַּרְזֶל הַיּוֹצֵא מִן הַכּוֹבַע כְּנֶגֶד הַחוֹטֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it was a kind of iron bar coming out of the helmet in front of the nose.

sources.quote: ונעשה לכסות בו הרגלים
sources.says: Metzudat David says it was made to cover the legs.

17:6.headline: The kidon between his shoulders: a neck guard or a javelin?
17:6.body: Rashi follows the Targum: a bronze spike from the helmet down his back, to guard his neck. Radak points to verse 45, where David names the כידון with sword and spear, and says it was a weapon for striking.

sources.quote: כְּמִין חֲנִית נְחֹשֶׁת בּוֹלֶטֶת מִן הַכּוֹבַע, וְנִמְשֶׁכֶת בֵּין כְּתֵפָיו, לְהָגֵן עַל צַוָּארוֹ מִן הַחֶרֶב
sources.says: Rashi says it was a bronze spike sticking out of the helmet down between his shoulders, to guard his neck from the sword.

sources.quote: נראה כי כידון זהו רומח כמו נטה בכידון הוא עשוי להכות בו לא להגן
sources.says: Radak says it seems to be a lance, made for striking, not for guarding.

sources.quote: זה הכידון איננו הכידון שזכר שהיה בין כתפיו אבל הוא דומה לחנית
sources.says: Ralbag says the כידון in verse 45 is not the one between his shoulders, but something like a spear.

17:12.headline: Jesse 'came among men': too old, or always with a following
17:12.body: בא באנשים is unclear. Radak reads it as among the old and weak, too frail to go to war. Rashi reads it as counted among the important men. The sages, quoted by Radak, say Jesse went out and came in with a crowd.

sources.quote: באנשי הזקנה והחולשה שלא היה יכול לצאת ולבוא
sources.says: Radak says it means among the old and weak, so he could not go out and come in.

sources.quote: נִמְנֶה בִּכְנֵסִיּוֹת הַחֲשׁוּבִים
sources.says: Rashi says he was counted in the gatherings of important men.

sources.quote: ורבותינו ז"ל אמרו בא באנשים זה ישי אבי דוד שיצא באוכלוסא ונכנס באוכלוסא
sources.says: Radak cites the sages: Jesse went out with a crowd and came in with a crowd.

17:16.headline: Morning and evening: the hours of the Shema
17:16.body: Goliath came out every morning and evening. Radak says the plain reason was to frighten Israel. Rashi and Radak cite the sages: he chose the times of the morning and evening Shema, to stop Israel from saying it.

sources.quote: כְּדֵי לְבַטְּלָם מִקְּרִיאַת שְׁמַע
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages: it was to keep them from reciting the Shema.

sources.quote: בקר וערב כדי להבהילם, ובדרש כדי לבטל מהם קרית שמע שחרית וערבית
sources.says: Radak says he came morning and evening to frighten them, and the midrash says to stop their morning and evening Shema.

17:18.headline: Bring back their 'pledge': news, pawned goods, or divorce papers
17:18.body: Jesse tells David to take his brothers' ערבה. Rashi reads it as a sign of their safety, to report home. Metzudat David reads it as goods they pawned for food, to redeem. The sages read it as divorce papers for their wives, given before battle.

sources.quote: וְאֶת עֲרוּבַת הַצָּלָתָם וּשְׁלוֹמָם, תִּקַּח בְּאָזְנֶיךָ וּבִלְבָבְךָ, וְתַגֵּד לִי
sources.says: Rashi says it means take note of how they are and whether they are safe, and tell me.

sources.quote: את משכונם אשר משכנו לצורך פרנסתם, תפדם מיד הממשכן
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means the pledges they pawned for food, which David should redeem.

sources.quote: גֵּט כְּרִיתוּת יִקַּח מֵאִתָּם וְיָבִיא לִנְשׁוֹתֵיהֶם, לְהַפְרִיד עֵרוּב שֶׁבֵּינוֹ לְבֵינָהּ
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages: bring a bill of divorce from them to their wives, to undo the bond between husband and wife.

17:25.headline: The victor's family made 'free': no taxes, or made nobles
17:25.body: The king promises to make the victor's family חפשי, free. Rashi and Metzudat David say free from the king's taxes and service. The Targum reads it as made great nobles, and Radak accepts both.

sources.quote: מִדְּבָרִים הָאֲמוּרִים בְּמִשְׁפְּטֵי הַמְּלוּכָה
sources.says: Rashi says free from the things listed in the laws of the king.

sources.quote: מבלי לעבוד עבודת המלך
sources.says: Metzudat David says free from working for the king.

sources.quote: חפשי ממשפט המלוכה וי"ת יעבד רברבין בישראל
sources.says: Radak says free from the king's laws, and the Targum renders it 'he will make them nobles in Israel'.

17:34.headline: The lamb David saved: some texts write 'this one'
17:34.body: David tells Saul a lion took a lamb, שה. Malbim cites a midrash that David made a belt from that lamb's skin and showed it to Saul. He adds that some texts even write זה, 'this', instead of שה, though the scholar of the Minchat Shai rejects it.

sources.quote: ובדרש שעשה לו אזור מעור השה לזכר הנס ועליו הראה כי זה הוא, וכן נמצא במקצת ספרים שהכתיב זה
sources.says: Malbim cites a midrash that David made a belt from the lamb's skin and pointed to it, and says some texts write זה here.

sources.quote: והמנחת שי ימאן בזה
sources.says: Malbim notes that the Minchat Shai rejects that reading.

17:36.headline: 'Also the lion, also the bear': the extra words add cubs
17:36.body: David says 'also the lion, also the bear'. Rashi and Radak cite the sages: each extra 'also' adds more beasts, so David fought the lion and the bear together with their young.

sources.quote: הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ רִבּוּיִין, אֲרִי וּשְׁנֵי גוּרָיו, וְדֹב וּשְׁנֵי יְלָדָיו
sources.says: Rashi says these words add more: a lion and two cubs, and a bear and two young.

sources.quote: מלמד שהיו שם חמש חיות רעות
sources.says: Radak cites the midrash that there were five wild beasts there.

17:38.headline: Saul's clothes, מדיו, fit David's size, מדה
17:38.body: Saul dresses David in מדיו, his clothes. Rashi hears מדה, measure, in the word: Saul's clothes shrank to David's size, though Saul was taller than anyone. Saul saw it and grew jealous.

sources.quote: נֶהֶפְכוּ לִהְיוֹת כְּמִדַּת דָּוִד מִשֶּׁנִּמְשַׁח בְּשֶׁמֶן הַמִּשְׁחָה
sources.says: Rashi says the clothes changed to David's measure, since he had been anointed with the holy oil.

sources.quote: ואמרו מדיו כמדתו וכתוב בשאול משכמו ומעלה גבוה מכל העם
sources.says: Radak cites the sages that the clothes were his size, though Saul was a head taller than all the people.

17:39.headline: David 'wanted' to walk in the armor, or refused to
17:39.body: ויאל usually means 'he wanted'. The Targum reads it as 'he did not want to go', and Rashi says some words can mean a thing and its opposite. Rashi also gives the plain reading: David wanted to try, found it too heavy, and took it off.

sources.quote: תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: ״וְלָא אָבָה לְמֵיזַל״. יֵשׁ תֵּיבוֹת מְשַׁמְּשׁוֹת לָשׁוֹן וְחִלּוּפוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum renders it 'he did not want to go', and that some words serve for a meaning and its opposite.

sources.quote: וַיּוֹאֶל לָלֶכֶת, רָצָה לָלֶכֶת וְלִנְסוֹת
sources.says: Rashi gives a second reading: he wanted to walk and try it.

sources.quote: ורצה, כמו (שמות ב כא): ויואל משה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means 'and he wanted', as in 'Moses agreed'.

17:40.headline: Why David picked exactly five stones
17:40.body: Radak cites the midrash on the number five. One stone for God, one for Aaron, and three for the patriarchs, each owed revenge on Goliath. Another reading says Goliath had mocked the five books of the Torah.

sources.quote: ובדרש למה חמשה אחד לשמו של הקב"ה ואחד לשמו של אהרן ושלשה לשלשת האבות
sources.says: Radak cites the midrash: why five? One for God, one for Aaron, and three for the three patriarchs.

sources.quote: שבזה וגידף וחרף חמשה חומשי תורה
sources.says: Radak cites another midrash: Goliath had scorned and mocked the five books of the Torah.

17:41.headline: Goliath 'came near', but David 'drew near'
17:41.body: Goliath קרב, comes near, while David ויגש, draws near (verse 40). Malbim says קרב is used between equals, and נגש when someone must gather courage before a greater power. David was the weaker one, so the text uses נגש for him.

sources.quote: הקריבה תהיה בין אנשים שוים, וההגשה הוא במקום שצריך להתחזק כמו לפני גדול לפני עריץ
sources.says: Malbim says קרב is used between equals, and נגש where one must take courage, as before a great or fearsome person.

sources.quote: ולכן דוד שהיה חלוש בערך הפלשתי כתוב אצלו ויגש
sources.says: Malbim says that is why David, weaker than the Philistine, is described with ויגש.

17:44.headline: Cattle don't eat people: Goliath's slip of the tongue
17:44.body: Goliath threatens to give David's flesh to 'the cattle of the field'. Radak notes that wild animals eat flesh, not cattle. Rashi cites the sages: David heard the slip and said this man has lost his mind and is already mine.

sources.quote: אֵין דֶּרֶךְ לִבְהֵמוֹת לֶאֱכֹל אָדָם, אָמַר דָּוִד: כְּבָר נִטְרְפָה דַּעְתּוֹ שֶׁל זֶה, שֶׁלִּי הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says cattle do not eat people, so David said: this man's mind is already gone, he is mine.

sources.quote: כמו ולחית השדה כי החיות אוכלות בשר לא הבהמות
sources.says: Radak says it means wild beasts, since beasts of prey eat flesh, not cattle.

17:56.headline: 'Whose son is this lad?': a law that was hidden from you
17:56.body: Saul first calls David נער, then עלם. Rashi cites the sages: Abner could not answer whether a descendant of Ruth the Moabite could marry in, so Saul told him the law was hidden, נתעלמה, from him. Malbim says עלם is a more respectful word than נער.

sources.quote: לְמַעְלָה כְּתִיב ׳הַנַּעַר׳, וְכָאן כָּתוּב ׳הָעֶלֶם׳, אָמַר לוֹ: הֲלָכָה זוֹ נִתְעַלְּמָה מִמְּךָ
sources.says: Rashi notes the switch from נער to עלם, and reads Saul as saying: this law has been hidden from you.

sources.quote: ששם עלם נכבד משם נער
sources.says: Malbim says the word עלם is more honorable than נער.

17:58.headline: 'Jesse the Bethlehemite': from Bethlehem, and a man of war
17:58.body: David answers that he is the son of Jesse בית הלחמי. Radak says the name means two things: Jesse came from Bethlehem, and he was a man of war, מלחמה. So David was telling Saul he was a warrior's son.

sources.quote: כי אבי נקרא בית הלחמי לשני דברים על שם מקומו בית לחם ועל שם שהיה איש מלחמה
sources.says: Radak says his father was called בית הלחמי for two reasons: his town Bethlehem, and being a man of war.

18:1.headline: From this verse on, Jonathan's name is spelled longer
18:1.body: Radak cites the Masorah, the old notes on spelling. Up to this verse the name is nearly always written יונתן, and from here to the end of the book it is written יהונתן.

sources.quote: המסרה מן ריש ספרא עד הכא יונתן בר מן ב'
sources.says: Radak says the Masorah notes that from the start of the book to here the name is spelled יונתן, except in two places.

sources.quote: ומן הכא עד סוף ספרא יהונתן
sources.says: Radak says from here to the end of the book it is spelled יהונתן.

18:6.headline: מחלות: dances, or instruments in the women's hands?
18:6.body: מחלות usually means dances, and the Aramaic Targum reads it so. Metzudat Zion says it names a musical instrument, as when Miriam's women went out with drums and מחלות, and Radak says the women held them in their hands.

sources.quote: והמחולות. שם כלי שיר, כמו (שמות טו כ): בתופים ובמחולות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the name of a musical instrument, as in with drums and מחולות in Exodus.

sources.quote: פי' והמחולות בידם וי"ת לשבח' בחנגיא
sources.says: Radak says it means with the מחולות in their hands, and notes the Targum translates it as dances.

18:7.headline: The women were joking, and Saul took it seriously
18:7.body: Malbim notes the verse calls them משחקות, women who play and joke, not singers. Their words had two faces and were meant for fun, but Saul took them at face value.

sources.quote: המשחקות שהן הדוברות דברי שחוק, דבור בעל שתי פנים לעורר צחוק ושמחה
sources.says: Malbim says the משחקות speak playful words, speech with two faces meant to stir laughter and joy.

sources.quote: אולם שאול לקח הדברים כפי פשטם
sources.says: Malbim says Saul took the words in their plain sense.

18:7.headline: Saul his thousands, David his ten thousands: of what?
18:7.body: Radak gives two readings: David killed tens of thousands of Philistines, or David alone fought as if ten thousand men were with him. Malbim adds that רבבות might hint at the stones David slung.

sources.quote: האלפים והרבבות של פלשתים
sources.says: Radak first says the thousands and ten thousands are of Philistines.

sources.quote: ודוד לבדו מכה בפלשתים מכה גדולה כאלו עמו רבבות
sources.says: Radak then says David alone struck the Philistines as hard as if ten thousand were with him.

sources.quote: או כוונו במלת רבבות על האבנים שרבה
sources.says: Malbim says the women may have meant by רבבות the stones he shot.

18:9.headline: Saul "eyed" David, a word built from the word for eye
18:9.body: עוין appears only here. Metzudat Zion hears both עין, eye, and עיון, hard thought, in it: Saul kept watching David and plotting against him with an evil eye.

sources.quote: עוין. מלשון עין, ומלשון עיון, ורוצה לומר תמיד היה מעיין ומחשב בו בעין רעה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from eye and from pondering: Saul always studied David and schemed against him with an evil eye.

sources.quote: עוין. (תרגום:) ״עין רעה״
sources.says: Rashi gives the translation evil eye.

sources.quote: כתוב בוי"ו וקרי ביו"ד ושניהם אחד ופירושו מביטו בעין רעה
sources.says: Radak says it is written with a vav and read with a yod, both meaning the same: looking at him with an evil eye.

18:10.headline: The evil spirit "crossed over" onto Saul
18:10.body: צלח often means to succeed. Here Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as passed over, as in crossing the Jordan, and the Aramaic Targum says the spirit came to rest on Saul.

sources.quote: ותצלח. ותעבור כמו וצלחו את הירדן
sources.says: Radak says it means passed over, as in they crossed the Jordan.

sources.quote: ותצלח. ועברה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means passed over.

sources.quote: ושרת רוח בישא מן קדם יי על שאול
sources.says: The Targum says an evil spirit from before the Lord rested on Saul.

18:10.headline: Saul "prophesied": he raved like a madman
18:10.body: ויתנבא usually means prophesied, but the Aramaic Targum says he raved. Rashi explains that a prophet and a madman both speak in hints others cannot follow, and Malbim says this verb form marks something less than true prophecy.

sources.quote: יתנבא. ״ואשתטי״ נביא ושוטה מדברים דברי רמזים שאינם נכרים
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum translates he raved, since a prophet and a madman both speak in unclear hints.

sources.quote: רוצה לומר היה מדבר דברי שטות, ואמר לשון נבואה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says he spoke nonsense, and the verse uses the word for prophecy.

sources.quote: דע כי כל מקום שכתוב פעל מתנבא בהתפעל מורה על נבואה בלתי גמורה
sources.says: Malbim says wherever this reflexive form of prophesy appears, it means an incomplete prophecy.

18:11.headline: "David and the wall": one throw, or a staged accident?
18:11.body: Rashi says Saul meant one blow strong enough to pass through David into the wall. Malbim says Saul wanted it to look as if he aimed at the wall, so David's death would seem an accident.

sources.quote: מכה אחת אכה, שיכנס החנית בדוד ובקיר
sources.says: Rashi says Saul meant to strike once so the spear would go into David and into the wall.

sources.quote: היה רוצה להכותו כבלתי מתכוין אל דוד רק אל הקיר, וכאילו הכהו בשגגה
sources.says: Malbim says Saul wanted to hit him as if aiming at the wall and not at David, as though by mistake.

18:14.headline: משכיל: David succeeded, or acted wisely?
18:14.body: משכיל comes from the word for good sense. Rashi reads it as succeeded, and Metzudat Zion explains why: success looks like acting wisely. Malbim keeps the plain sense here: David did everything with thought and knowledge.

sources.quote: משכיל. מצליח
sources.says: Rashi says it means succeeding.

sources.quote: ישכיל. יצליח, כי המצליח נראה הוא כעושה בהשכל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means succeed, because one who succeeds looks like one who acts with sense.

sources.quote: והיה משכיל רצה לומר עושה הכל בהשכל ודעת
sources.says: Malbim says it means he did everything with understanding and knowledge.

18:21.headline: "Through two you will marry into my family": which two?
18:21.body: Rashi and Radak, following the Aramaic, read it as through one of my two daughters. Malbim reads it as Saul claiming he still stands by both matches, so David is tied to him through both.

sources.quote: שתי בנות יש לי, באחת מהן תתחתן בי
sources.says: Rashi says Saul meant: I have two daughters, and through one of them you will marry into my family.

sources.quote: בשתים תתחתן בי. כתרגומו בחדא מן תרתי
sources.says: Radak follows the Targum: with one of two.

sources.quote: ואני עודני מסכים גם על נשואי מירב, עד שאני מחותן לך מצד שתיהם
sources.says: Malbim says Saul claimed he still agreed to the match with Merab, so he was David's in-law through both.

18:27.headline: They "filled" the count: presented, or paid in full?
18:27.body: וימלאום means they filled them. Rashi gives the Old French word for presented; Radak and Metzudat David say they paid the full count, two hundred when Saul had asked for one hundred.

sources.quote: וימלאום. פרישנטי״ר בלע״ז
sources.says: Rashi gives the Old French word for presented.

sources.quote: ופירוש וימלאום השלימום כלומר כל המאתים הביאו לפניו
sources.says: Radak says it means they completed it, bringing all two hundred before him.

sources.quote: וימלאום. השלים את כל המאתים, עם שלא אמר כי אם מאה
sources.says: Metzudat David says David completed all two hundred, though Saul had asked for only a hundred.

18:30.headline: His name grew precious: a midrash credits David's knowledge of law
18:30.body: Plainly, people spoke of David with great honor. Radak brings a midrash: the Philistines attacked thinking a new groom could not go to war, but David knew that in a war of duty even a groom goes out.

sources.quote: שכל מי שהיה מזכיר שמו היה מזכירו ביקר ובכבוד רב
sources.says: Ralbag says whoever mentioned his name did so with great honor.

sources.quote: ובדרש וייקר שמו בהלכה
sources.says: Radak brings a midrash that his name became precious through his knowledge of law.

sources.quote: ולא היו יודעים כי דוד חכם היה ודורש במה דברים אמורים במלחמת רשות אבל במלחמת מצוה הכל יוצאין
sources.says: Radak says the Philistines did not know David was wise and taught that the groom's exemption applies only to an optional war, while in a commanded war everyone goes out.

2:1.headline: 'Hannah prayed', though her words sound like a song of praise
2:1.body: Malbim asks why the verse says 'prayed' when she only gives praise. Metzudat David says she praises first and the real prayer comes at the end; Radak says prayer mostly looks to the future, and her song is prophecy.

sources.quote: כפי הגלוי אין כאן תפלה רק הלל ושבח שיר וזמרה והיה לו לאמר ותשר חנה
sources.says: Malbim asks why it says 'prayed' when this is only praise and song, and should have said 'Hannah sang'.

sources.quote: עצם התפלה היא בסוף אמריה, ובתחלה סדרה שבחו של מקום
sources.says: Metzudat David says the prayer itself is at the end, after she first sets out God's praise.

sources.quote: ולכך התחיל בה בלשון ותתפלל כי לשון התפלה יפול ברוב על הענינים העתידים
sources.says: Radak says it opens with 'prayed' because prayer is mostly about things to come.

2:2.headline: Tzur: a rock, an artist, or the source of all things?
2:2.body: Metzudat Zion reads צור as strength, like a rock. Rashi reads it as ציר, an artist who shapes a form inside a form; Maimonides says God is called צור because He is the cause of everything else.

sources.quote: צור. ענין חוזק, והוא מלשון צור וסלע
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says tzur means strength, from the word for rock.

sources.quote: אין ציר כאלהינו, הצר צורה בתוך צורה
sources.says: Rashi reads it as 'there is no artist like our God', who forms a shape within a shape.

sources.quote: כי הוא הראשית והסיבה הפועלת לכל מה שזולתו
sources.says: Maimonides says God is called Tzur because He is the beginning and the cause of all else, and cites this verse.

2:3.headline: 'Lofty, lofty': why the word is said twice
2:3.body: Metzudat David says the doubling shows great and lasting arrogance. Malbim reads it as the claim that God is too high to care about lowly people.

sources.quote: וכפלה המלה, להורות על גאוה גדולה והתמדתה
sources.says: Metzudat David says she doubled the word to show great pride that keeps going.

sources.quote: שה' הוא גבוה גבוה רצה לומר שהוא מרומם ומנושא מלהשגיח בשפלים
sources.says: Malbim says it means the claim that God is so high that He does not watch over the lowly.

2:3.headline: A God of 'knowledges': why the plural?
2:3.body: Radak says the plural means God knows every person's thoughts at once, without becoming many or changing. Malbim says the verse answers philosophers who held that changing knowledge cannot belong to God.

sources.quote: ואמרה דעות לשון רבים כלומר כל דעות בני אדם ידעם כאחד בלא רבוי ובלא שינוי אצלו
sources.says: Radak says the plural means God knows all human thoughts as one, without multiplying or changing.

sources.quote: ואם כן אם ידעם תמיד יתחייב כי תשתנה ידיעתו
sources.says: Malbim gives the objection: if God always knew changing things, His knowledge would have to change.

2:3.headline: Written 'not', read 'to Him': two readings in one word
2:3.body: The word is written ולא, 'and not', but read ולו, 'and to Him'. Radak explains both: people's deeds do not come about unless God wills it, and deeds belong to God alone.

sources.quote: ופירוש הכתוב כי לא נתכנו עלילות בני אדם אם לא יחפוץ האל ופי' הקרי כי לו לבדו נתכנו העלילות
sources.says: Radak says the written form means people's deeds are not done unless God wants, and the read form means deeds are His alone.

sources.quote: כל מעשי האדם נמנין לפניו
sources.says: Rashi says all of a person's deeds are counted before God.

2:5.headline: 'The barren one bore seven': seven adds up to Samuel
2:5.body: Rashi brings a view that שבעה, seven, has the same number value as שמואל, Samuel: both add up to 377. Malbim says seven is just a way of saying many.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: שבעה, בגימטריא כמנין שמואל
sources.says: Rashi brings those who say 'seven' equals 'Samuel' in number value.

sources.quote: ובדרש עד עקרה ילדה שבעה שמואל בגימטריא במספר שבעה
sources.says: Radak cites the midrash that Samuel's name equals 'seven' in number value.

sources.quote: כי דרך לתפוס מספר שבעה על מספר גדול
sources.says: Malbim says seven is commonly used for a large number.

2:6.headline: Down to Sheol and up again: rescue, or rising from the dead?
2:6.body: Ralbag says Hannah foretold the dead coming back to life, with שאול meaning the grave. Radak first reads it as keeping a person alive, or as hard times and relief, and only last as the rising of the dead.

sources.quote: כאן נתנבאה על תחיית המתים בביאור
sources.says: Ralbag says here she clearly prophesied the resurrection of the dead.

sources.quote: כי הרצון בשאול קבר
sources.says: Ralbag says Sheol means the grave.

sources.quote: מחיה שמעמידו בחיים ומאריך ימיו כשירצה
sources.says: Radak says 'gives life' can mean God keeps a person alive and lengthens his days.

sources.quote: או הוא רמז לצרות ולרווחות
sources.says: Radak says it may hint at troubles and relief.

2:8.headline: The 'pillars of the earth' may be righteous people
2:8.body: Metzudat Zion says מצקי are the pillars that hold the earth up, from ויציקו, 'they set down'. Radak adds that the pillars are the righteous, whose merit keeps the world standing.

sources.quote: ורצה לומר, היסודות והעמודים שהם מצבי הארץ ומעמידים אותה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says they are the foundations and pillars that hold up the earth.

sources.quote: ומצוקי ארץ הם הצדיקים כי בזכותם מתקיים התבל
sources.says: Radak says the pillars of the earth are the righteous, whose merit keeps the world going.

2:10.headline: 'Against him' is written 'they went up': even to heaven
2:10.body: The word is read עליו, 'against him', but written עלו, 'they went up'. Rashi reads the written form: even if they climb to heaven, God thunders on them and brings them down.

sources.quote: עלו כתיב, אפלו עלו בשמים, מרעים עליהם ומורידם
sources.says: Rashi says it is written 'alu': even if they went up to heaven, He thunders on them and brings them down.

sources.quote: עליו על כל אחד ממריביו
sources.says: Radak reads it as 'against him', on each one of God's enemies.

2:10.headline: Hannah speaks of an anointed king before Israel had one
2:10.body: Israel had no king yet. Radak says Hannah spoke by prophecy or tradition, hinting that her son Samuel would anoint the king; Metzudat David says she meant David.

sources.quote: ואמרה חנה זה על דרך נבואה או דרך קבלה כי היתה קבלה אצלה כי עתיד להיות מלך בישראל
sources.says: Radak says Hannah said this by prophecy, or from a tradition that Israel would one day have a king.

sources.quote: רמזה בזה שעל ידי שמואל בנה יהיה מלך בישראל והוא ימשחנו
sources.says: Radak says she hinted that a king would come through her son Samuel, who would anoint him.

sources.quote: וירם קרן משיחו. על דוד אמרה
sources.says: Metzudat David says she said this about David.

2:11.headline: Serving God 'before Eli': serving a teacher counts as serving God
2:11.body: The verse says the boy served God 'before Eli the priest'. Rashi learns from this that serving a Torah scholar is like serving God's presence.

sources.quote: מכאן למשמש פני תלמידי חכמים, כמשמש פני השכינה
sources.says: Rashi says we learn that one who serves Torah scholars is like one who serves the Divine Presence.

sources.quote: כלומר שהיה עלי מלמדו עבודת ה'
sources.says: Radak says it means Eli was teaching him how to serve God.

2:17.headline: Minchah here covers every offering, each one a gift
2:17.body: The sons were taking meat, so the word must be wider than a flour offering. Metzudat Zion says מנחה here covers all the offerings, since each is a gift.

sources.quote: מנחת. המלה ההיא כולל כל הקרבנות שהמה למנחה ולדורון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word includes all the offerings, since they are a present and a gift.

sources.quote: את מנחת ה'. כתרגום ית קורבניא דה'
sources.says: Radak follows the Targum, which renders it 'the offerings of the Lord'.

2:18.headline: Samuel wore an ephod, though he was no priest
2:18.body: Metzudat Zion says this was not the high priest's ephod but a linen garment like it, worn by people who served God, as David later did. Rashi follows the Targum, which calls it a kind of robe.

sources.quote: ויחגרו בו עובדי ה׳ להשתנות משאר בני אדם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says servants of God wore it to stand apart from other people.

sources.quote: ששמואל הגם שלא היה בן הכהן הגדול ולא כהן
sources.says: Malbim notes that Samuel was not the high priest's son and not a priest.

sources.quote: והוא לשון מעיל
sources.says: Rashi says, following the Targum, that it means a robe.

2:22.headline: Did Eli's sons lie with the women, or just delay them?
2:22.body: Rashi gives the plain meaning, then the sages: the sons held up the women's bird offerings, and Scripture counts that as if they lay with them. Ralbag notes the prophet later scolds them only for the meat.

sources.quote: מתוך ששהו את קניהן, והם היו ממתינות עד שתראן קניהן קרבין, מעלה עליהם כאלו שכבום
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages that the sons delayed the women's bird offerings, and Scripture counts it as if they lay with them.

sources.quote: ולא מצאנו שגנה אותם רק על החטא שזכר תחלה
sources.says: Ralbag argues the prophet blames them only for the first sin, so this cannot mean adultery.

2:24.headline: 'Passing on' a bad report, or driving the people away?
2:24.body: Rashi and Maimonides read מעברים as spreading a report, the way sound passes through the air. Radak also offers: you are making God's people stay away from the Tent because of your greed.

sources.quote: שמועה שעם ה׳ מעבירים עליכם, לשון ״ויעבירו קול במחנה״
sources.says: Rashi says it is a report God's people are passing around about you, as in 'they passed a call through the camp'.

sources.quote: אחר כך הושאל להתפשטות הקולות באוויר
sources.says: Maimonides says the word for passing was borrowed for sound spreading through the air, and cites this verse.

sources.quote: שאתם מעבירים עם ה' מלבא באהל מועד מפני החמס שאתם עושים להם בקרבנותיהם
sources.says: Radak says you are turning God's people away from the Tent because of the wrong you do with their offerings.

2:25.headline: Pillel: to judge, and to pray, from one root
2:25.body: Rashi says ופללו means 'judge him', as in בפלילים, 'by judges'. Radak says the next word, יתפלל, can mean either pleading his case or praying for him.

sources.quote: ופללו. לשון משפט, כמו ״ונתן בפלילים״
sources.says: Rashi says the word means judgment, as in 'he shall pay as the judges decide'.

sources.quote: מי יתפלל בעבורו כלומר מי יכנס למשפט בעבורו עם השם ית', ויש לפרשו לשון תפלה ובקשה
sources.says: Radak says it means who will enter judgment with God for him, or it can mean prayer and pleading.

2:27.headline: 'Did I reveal Myself?' A question, or a firm statement?
2:27.body: The ה at the start can ask a question or stress a fact. Ralbag reads 'I surely revealed Myself', Radak's father read it as an outraged question, and Rashi learns from it that Aaron prophesied in Egypt.

sources.quote: אין הה"א ה"א התימה אבל הוא ה"א האמתית
sources.says: Ralbag says the heh is not a question of surprise but one that affirms.

sources.quote: ואדוני אבי ז"ל פירשו לתמיהה
sources.says: Radak says his father read it as a question of outrage.

sources.quote: מכאן שנתנבא אהרן במצרים
sources.says: Rashi says we learn from here that Aaron prophesied in Egypt.

2:29.headline: 'To fatten yourselves': a feast, and a charge against Eli too
2:29.body: Rashi reads להבריאכם as feasting; Metzudat Zion and Radak read it as fattening, like fat Eglon. Radak notes it says 'yourselves', not 'them', since Eli must also have eaten what his sons took.

sources.quote: להבריאכם. לשון סעודה
sources.says: Rashi says the word means a meal, as in Tamar preparing food.

sources.quote: להבריאכם. ענין שומן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means fatness, as with Eglon.

sources.quote: ולא אמר להבריאם, כי אי אפשר שלא היה עלי אוכל ממה שהיו בניו אוכלים
sources.says: Radak says it does not say 'to fatten them', because Eli surely ate from what his sons ate.

2:30.headline: God honors those who honor Him; the scorners shame themselves
2:30.body: God says 'I will honor', but not 'I will shame'. Rashi and Radak say the scorners fall into shame by themselves once God turns away from them.

sources.quote: ואמר יקלו ולא אמר אקל כמו שאמר אכבד כי הם יקלו מעצמם בהסתירי פני מהם
sources.says: Radak says it says 'they will be shamed' and not 'I will shame', because they shame themselves when God hides His face.

sources.quote: ובזי יקלו. מאליהם, משאסתלק מהם
sources.says: Rashi says they will be shamed on their own, once God departs from them.

2:31.headline: 'I will cut off your arm': their force taken away
2:31.body: Metzudat Zion says the arm stands for strength. Rashi ties it to the sons' words in verse 16, 'I will take it by force': that very strength will be cut off.

sources.quote: זרועך. ענין חוזק, כי החוזק היא בזרוע
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the arm means strength, since strength is in the arm.

sources.quote: החוזק שיש לכם בביתי, שאתם אומרים ואם לא לקחתי בחזקה
sources.says: Rashi says it is the strength you hold in My house, when you say 'if not, I will take it by force'.

sources.quote: זרועך. חוזקך כלומר אורך החיים
sources.says: Radak says the arm means strength, that is, long life.

2:31.headline: No 'elder' in your house: no old men, or no leaders?
2:31.body: Ralbag and Radak say no one in Eli's family would live to old age. Metzudat David reads זקן as a ruler, and the sages as a sage: no one of Eli's house would sit on the high court.

sources.quote: ירצה בזה שלא יהיה בהם מי שיזקין אבל ימותו בחורים
sources.says: Ralbag says none of them will grow old; they will die young.

sources.quote: רצה לומר: מושל ושר, כי המושלים והשרים נקראו זקני העם
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means a ruler, since rulers are called elders of the people.

sources.quote: ורבו' פירשו חכם כמו והדרת פני זקן ר"ל שלא יהיה מבית עלי סמוך בסנהדרין
sources.says: Radak says the sages read it as a sage: no one from Eli's house would be ordained to the Sanhedrin.

2:32.headline: Tzar: a rival priest like a rival wife, or a tight squeeze?
2:32.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read צר as a rival, the word for a second wife: another priestly family would serve beside Eli's. Ralbag reads it as narrow: Eli's house would be squeezed out of the good times.

sources.quote: וראית צרתך בצדך בתוך מעוני, כאשה הרואה צרתה עמה בבית
sources.says: Rashi says you will see your rival beside you in My house, like a woman who sees her rival wife with her at home.

sources.quote: כמו ששתי נשים לאיש אחד תקראנה צרות, כמו כן יקראו שני כהנים גדולים זה לזה בלשון צר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says just as two wives of one man are called rivals, two high priests are called rivals.

sources.quote: שכבר תביט מקום צר דחוק לך
sources.says: Ralbag says you will see a narrow, tight place for you.

2:33.headline: Letters swapped: ladiv stands for ledaiv, 'to grieve'
2:33.body: This form appears only here. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say its letters are switched, so it means לדאיב, to make the soul grieve, as in דאבון נפש.

sources.quote: ולאדיב. כמו ולדאיב
sources.says: Rashi says ladiv is like ledaiv.

sources.quote: הוא הפוך, כמו ולדאיב, והוא מענין צער ותוגה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the letters are reversed, like ledaiv, meaning pain and sorrow.

sources.quote: הפוך מן דאבון נפש
sources.says: Radak says it is reversed from 'sorrow of soul'.

2:35.headline: Ne'eman: a faithful priest, and a house that lasts
2:35.body: The verse uses נאמן twice. Of the priest it means faithful; of his house, Radak and Metzudat Zion say it means lasting, as in 'a peg in a firm place'.

sources.quote: בית נאמן. פי' קיים כמו במקום נאמן
sources.says: Radak says a ne'eman house means a lasting one, as in 'in a firm place'.

sources.quote: נאמן. מתקיים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ne'eman means enduring.

sources.quote: בית קבוע לו ולזרעו אחריו
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means a fixed house for him and his descendants.

2:36.headline: Agorat: a small silver coin, or a wage?
2:36.body: Metzudat Zion says the א is extra and the word is גרה, a small silver coin. Radak also reports a view that links it to the Aramaic אגרא, wages.

sources.quote: לאגורת. האל״ף נוספת, והוא כמו גרה, שהיא מטבע של כסף
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the aleph is extra and it is like gerah, a silver coin.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים אותו מתרגום שכר אגרא
sources.says: Radak says some explain it from the Aramaic word for wages, agra.

sources.quote: בשביל להשתכר מעה כסף
sources.says: Rashi says it means to earn a silver coin.

21:2.headline: Did the priest tremble in fear, or rush out to David?
21:2.body: The verb חרד usually means to tremble. Radak says it can also mean to hurry out to meet someone, or it can mean real fear, because David came alone.

sources.quote: והוא לשון תנועה כמו ויחרדו זקני העיר לקראתו
sources.says: Radak reads it as quick movement, like the elders who hurried to meet Samuel, and also allows the plain sense of fear.

sources.quote: מיהר בחרדה לקראתו
sources.says: Metzudat David says the priest hurried anxiously to meet him.

21:3.headline: Did David tell his men, or make them hurry ahead?
21:3.body: The word looks like 'I made known'. Rashi reads it as 'I put them to trouble': David made his young men run ahead to a secret place.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן טֹרַח, הַנְּעָרִים אֲשֶׁר יָצְאוּ עִמִּי, הִטְרַחְתִּים
sources.says: Rashi says the word means trouble: David made the young men who left with him hurry ahead.

sources.quote: כמו הודעתי או הוא מן הדומה למרובע
sources.says: Radak reads it as 'I told them', meaning he told them to go ahead and wait for him.

21:3.headline: 'Such-and-such place' comes from a word for hidden
21:3.body: פלני is the word for 'so-and-so'. Rashi and Radak trace it to יפלא, a thing hidden or too hard to know. David is keeping the place secret.

sources.quote: פְּלֹנִי. כְּמוֹ ״כִּי יִפָּלֵא
sources.says: Rashi links the word to 'if a matter is too hard for you' and says it means covered over.

sources.quote: פלוני מן כי יפלא ממך דבר
sources.says: Radak says it comes from the same root as 'if a matter is too hard for you', meaning a hidden place.

21:3.headline: A place with no name, from the word for mute
21:3.body: Rashi says אלמוני means nameless, a place David does not want to mention. Metzudat Zion ties it to אלם, mute: a place one keeps silent about.

sources.quote: מֵאֵין שֵׁם, שֶׁאֵינִי חָפֵץ לְהַזְכִּיר
sources.says: Rashi says it means without a name, because David does not want to say it.

sources.quote: מלשון, אלם, ורצה לומר אין לגלות המקום ולאומרה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from the word for mute: the place must not be revealed or spoken.

21:6.headline: Is the 'ordinary' thing the journey or the bread?
21:6.body: דרך can mean a road or a way of being. Radak reads it as 'we set out on an ordinary trip'. Rashi reads it as 'the bread is now close to ordinary bread'.

sources.quote: וְהַלֶּחֶם מִשֶּׁנִּסְתַּלֵּק מֵעַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן וְהִקְטִירוּ הַבָּזִיכִין, קָרוֹב הוּא לִהְיוֹת חֻלִּין
sources.says: Rashi says that once the bread was taken off the table and the incense burned, it was close to ordinary bread.

sources.quote: אף על פי שיצאנו דרך חול שלא היינו סבורים שהיינו צריכים ללחם קדש
sources.says: Radak says it means they left on an ordinary trip, not expecting to need holy bread.

21:7.headline: The sages read a miracle into the 'warm' bread
21:7.body: The verse says warm bread replaced the old. The sages, cited by Rashi and Radak, say the old bread was still as warm when it was removed as on the day it was set out.

sources.quote: חֹם בְּיוֹם הִלָּקְחוֹ, גַּם בְּיוֹם סִלּוּקוֹ, חֹם כְּיוֹם סִדּוּרוֹ
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages: on the day it was removed, the bread was as warm as the day it was arranged.

sources.quote: נס גדול נעשה בלחם הפנים סלוקו חם כסדורו
sources.says: Radak cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: a great miracle kept the showbread warm until it was removed.

21:8.headline: Chief of the shepherds, or head of the court?
21:8.body: The plain sense is that Doeg was in charge of Saul's herdsmen. Rashi gives the sages' reading that he was the head of the court. Radak calls that a sermon, not the plain sense.

sources.quote: אַבִּיר הָרֹעִים. אַב בֵּית דִּין
sources.says: Rashi says the 'mightiest of the shepherds' was the head of the court.

sources.quote: שהיה אב ב"ד וזהו דרך דרש
sources.says: Radak says the head-of-court reading is a sermonic one.

sources.quote: גדול רועי המקנה אשר לשאול וממונה עליהם
sources.says: Ralbag says he was the chief of Saul's herdsmen and in charge of them.

21:8.headline: Doeg was called 'the Edomite' for where he lived
21:8.body: Radak says Doeg was called Edomite because he lived in Edom, the way Uriah was called the Hittite. Metzudat Zion adds that he was an Israelite by birth.

sources.quote: גר בארץ אדום לפיכך קראו אדומי וכן אוריה החתי
sources.says: Radak says he lived in the land of Edom, so he was called Edomite, like Uriah the Hittite.

sources.quote: שהיה גר באדום, אבל היה ישראל מלידה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says he lived in Edom but was an Israelite by birth.

21:9.headline: With an odd vowel, 'there is not' becomes 'is there?'
21:9.body: ואין normally means 'and there is not'. Rashi reads it as 'and if there is', and Radak says it is a question: is there a sword here for me?

sources.quote: וְאִין יֶשׁ פֹּה. וְאִם יֵשׁ פֹּה
sources.says: Rashi says the word means 'and if there is'.

sources.quote: בחירק כמו ואין בצרי והוא דרך שאלה
sources.says: Radak says the word has an unusual vowel and is asked as a question.

21:9.headline: A word found only here, read from its setting as 'urgent'
21:9.body: Radak says נחוץ appears nowhere else, so its meaning comes from the context: in a hurry. The Targum also translates it 'in haste'.

sources.quote: ענינו לפי מקומו מהיר ואין לו חבר וכן תירגם יונתן בבהילו
sources.says: Radak says that from its place it means hurried, that it has no match elsewhere, and that the Targum renders it 'in haste'.

sources.quote: ענין מהירות רב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means great haste.

21:10.headline: Behind the ephod, or after asking God through the ephod?
21:10.body: אחרי can mean behind a place or after a time. Rashi and the Targum read it as time: the priest offered the sword after asking God for David through the ephod.

sources.quote: אַחַר שֶׁשָּׁאֲלוּ בָּאוּרִים וְתֻמִּים, אָמַר לוֹ כֵּן
sources.says: Rashi says it means after the priest asked for him through the Urim and Tummim.

sources.quote: ונכון הוא בעיני פירושו אבל אינו דרך פשט הפסוק לפי מקומו
sources.says: Radak likes the Targum's reading but says the plain sense is that the sword hung behind where the ephod was kept.

21:11.headline: Achish here, Avimelech in Psalms: one king, two names
21:11.body: The Book of Psalms calls this king Avimelech. Radak says he either had two names, or Avimelech was a title for every Philistine king, like Pharaoh in Egypt.

sources.quote: או אבימלך שם כנוי לכל מלכי פלשתים כמו פרעה מלך מצרים
sources.says: Radak says Psalms calls him Avimelech, and either he had two names or Avimelech was a title for all Philistine kings.

21:12.headline: King of which land? Achish's servants mean their own
21:12.body: Goliath had promised that if he lost, the Philistines would serve Israel. Rashi says the servants meant that David beat Goliath, so by that deal he should be king of Philistia.

sources.quote: אֵין לְךָ אֶלָּא שֶׁתֵּרֵד מִכִּסְאֲךָ, וְיִהְיֶה מֶלֶךְ הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת
sources.says: Rashi says the servants told Achish that by Goliath's terms he must step down and David should be king of this land.

sources.quote: מלך הארץ הזאת של פלשתים שכפי התנאי שהתנה גלית אנחנו עבדים למנצח הפלשתי
sources.says: Malbim says they meant king of the Philistine land, since by Goliath's condition they were slaves to whoever beat him.

21:16.headline: Achish already had madness at home, say the sages
21:16.body: Achish asks, 'Am I short of madmen?' A midrash cited by Radak says his wife and daughter were mad and screaming inside while David raved outside.

sources.quote: ובדרש כי אשתו של אכיש ובתו היו משוגעות וצועקות ומשטות מבפנים ודוד צועק ומשטה מבחוץ
sources.says: Radak cites a midrash that Achish's wife and daughter were mad inside the house while David acted mad outside.

sources.quote: שהיתה אשתו ובתו משוגעות
sources.says: Metzudat David cites the midrash that his wife and daughter were mad.

23:5.headline: Why did a raiding army have livestock with it?
23:5.body: Radak asks how the Philistines had cattle at a battle. He says David beat them and chased the runaways back into Philistine land, and took their herds there.

sources.quote: איך היו מקניהם במלחמה אלא כשהכה דוד מהם מכה גדולה רדף אחרי הנסים מהם עד ארץ פלשתים ונהג את מקניהם
sources.says: Radak asks how they had livestock in battle, and answers that after the great defeat David chased the fleeing men into Philistine land and drove off their livestock.

23:6.headline: The ephod 'came down' in his hand, almost by chance
23:6.body: Targum Jonathan reads ירד as 'he brought down'. Radak reads it plainly as 'it came down': Abiathar fled grabbing whatever he could, and the ephod happened to be among his things, by God's design.

sources.quote: אֵפוֹדָא אָחִית בִּידֵיהּ
sources.says: Targum Jonathan renders it 'brought down an ephod in his hand'.

sources.quote: כשלקח כליו עמו בברחו לא השגיח מה לקח ומה הניח כאדם בורח והיתה סבה מאת ה' והיה האפוד בדרך מקרה בין כליו לפיכך אמר ירד ולא אמר הוריד
sources.says: Radak says that in his flight he did not notice what he took, and God arranged that the ephod was by chance among his things, so it says 'came down' and not 'brought down'.

sources.quote: הוא לא כיון לקחת אפוד כי נמלט אז על נפשו רק האפוד ירד בידו בהשגחת ה'
sources.says: Malbim says Abiathar did not mean to take the ephod, since he was running for his life, but it came into his hand by God's providence.

23:7.headline: A one-time verb: God has 'handed him over' to me
23:7.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion say נכר here means 'delivered'. Malbim notes it has no match in the Bible and links it to נכרי, foreigner, while Ralbag says it means God took away David's good judgment.

sources.quote: נִכַּר אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים בְּיָדִי. הִסְגִּיר
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'handed over'.

sources.quote: מסר, וכן (דברים לב ל): כי צורם מכרם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means delivered, as in Deuteronomy 32:30.

sources.quote: ולא נמצא לו ריע במקרא, ונראה שמשתתף עם נכר מענין נכרי
sources.says: Malbim says the word has no partner in Scripture and seems related to the word for foreigner, so Saul can now treat David like a foreign enemy.

sources.quote: שהש״י הסיר ממנו ההכרה והבחינה כדי שיפול בידי
sources.says: Ralbag says it means God removed David's discernment so that he would fall into Saul's hands.

23:9.headline: Saul is 'plowing' evil, or quietly hiding it
23:9.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion read מחריש as plotting, from 'do not plow evil against your neighbor' in Proverbs. Malbim reads it as keeping silent: Saul hid who his target was, but David understood.

sources.quote: עניינו חושב כמו אל תחרוש על רעך רעה
sources.says: Radak says it means plotting, as in 'do not plow evil against your neighbor'.

sources.quote: ענין מחשבה, כמו (משלי ג כט): אל תחרוש על רעך רעה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means scheming, as in Proverbs 3:29.

sources.quote: ודוד הבין ששאול מחריש ומעלים הדבר וכוונתו עליו
sources.says: Malbim says David understood that Saul was keeping quiet and hiding the matter, and that he was the target.

sources.quote: כְּמִין יָת בִּישְׁתָּא
sources.says: Rashi cites the Targum: he lies in wait with evil.

23:11.headline: David asked two questions but got one answer
